stops.name: Trujillo, the castle above the plain
stops.campa: Under the granite castle of Trujillo, in the harsh table-land of Extremadura, Francisco is born to Captain Gonzalo Pizarro and a servant girl, Francisca González, out of wedlock and out of any house's notice. The chroniclers will later dispute the year (1471, 1475, 1478), as they dispute so much of him, but not the shame of his birth nor the indifference that follows it. No font records the day. He grows up in his father's shadow and his mother's poverty, one bastard among the many Extremadura will send across the Ocean to make himself a name by the sword alone.

stops.name: Trujillo, the swineherd legend
stops.campa: He can neither read nor write; no one troubles to teach him. The tradition sets him to herding his father's (or another man's) swine on the stony commons outside the walls, so destitute, the story insists, that he is reduced like the prodigal son to eating the very swill thrown to the animals in his charge. It is a legend built to be outgrown: the same hands that cannot hold a pen will hold a sword well enough to unmake an empire, and the chroniclers who scorn the swineherd will not scorn the marqués he becomes.

stops.name: Seville, the gate to the Indies
stops.campa: He needs little encouragement to abandon the ignoble trade of the pigsty. Word runs through Extremadura of a New World across the Ocean where even base-born men win encomiendas and titles; his own kinsman's line, the Cortés of Medellín, will send another such son within the decade. Pizarro walks the short road down to Seville, city of the Casas de Contratación, of caravels loading for Hispaniola on the tide of the Guadalquivir, and takes service, a soldier with no name of his own, in the fleet that Governor Nicolás de Ovando is gathering for the Indies.

stops.name: Sanlúcar de Barrameda, Ovando's fleet of thirty sail
stops.campa: Thirty ships and twenty-five hundred men clear the bar of the Guadalquivir at Sanlúcar under Governor Ovando, the largest fleet yet sent to the Indies: among them the unlettered Pizarro, one soldier among the crowd, and the young Bartolomé de las Casas, who will later write against everything this fleet is sailing to do. Christopher Columbus himself, on his fourth and last voyage, quits the same roadstead weeks after them, outbound for a coast neither man yet imagines they share. Pizarro's Ocean has begun.

stops.name: Santo Domingo, landfall among the first conquistadors
stops.campa: The fleet makes the harbor of Santo Domingo, capital of the Spanish Isle, where the same stone tower that will one day hold Columbus under arrest already stands above the Ozama. Pizarro steps ashore an anonymous soldier of fortune among hundreds like him, and spends the better part of a decade in the wars and repartimientos of Hispaniola and the pearl coast, learning the trade that will make him: how a handful of armored men break the will of a hundred unarmored ones, and how little the Crown asks of the manner of it.

stops.name: Urabá, the doomed colony of San Sebastián
stops.campa: Under Alonso de Ojeda, Pizarro sails to the Gulf of Urabá to seed a colony on the Tierra Firme itself: San Sebastián, a stockade fort raised against hostile bowmen who dip their arrows in a poison that kills within the hour. Hunger and the poisoned shafts empty the garrison faster than any battle; Ojeda sails back to Hispaniola for relief and does not return. Pizarro is left in command of the survivors with orders to hold fifty days and no longer. He holds the ground until the ships of Enciso and Balboa find him, half the company already dead.

stops.name: Santa María la Antigua del Darién, the first city of Tierra Firme
stops.campa: The survivors of San Sebastián cross the gulf with Balboa and found, on ground the Indians call Darién, the first permanent Spanish town of the American mainland: a stockade, a church, a plaza traced in the mud. Pizarro serves here as one of Balboa's captains through the campaigns that break the chiefs of the isthmus one after another: Cémaco, Careta, Ponca, learning the geography of Tierra Firme and the rumor, repeated by every cacique they plunder, of a sea beyond the mountains and a kingdom of gold still farther south.

stops.name: The Sierra of Quarequa, the ascent to the South Sea
stops.campa: With a hundred and ninety Spaniards and a thousand native bearers, Balboa cuts south from Darién through jungle, swamp, and the cacique Quarequa's spears, and climbs the last bare ridge alone, ahead of the column, so that no other Christian eye takes the sight before his. Pizarro is among the hundred he has chosen for this march. At the top Balboa falls to his knees; behind him the company crowds up and falls to its knees also, and there below them, silver in the noon light, lies a sea no European has ever seen. They sing the Te Deum on the ridge.

stops.name: The Gulf of San Miguel, Balboa wades into the new ocean
stops.campa: Four days down from the ridge to the shingle, Balboa wades waist-deep into the tide with sword and banner and claims the South Sea, its islands, and every coast it washes for the Crown of Castile, in the hearing of Pizarro and the rest of the company drawn up on the strand. It is the discovery on which every later thing in this life depends: the sea that will one day carry three small ships south along an unmapped coast, past Tumbes, toward an empire richer than any cacique of the isthmus has yet described.

stops.name: Acla, the arrest of Balboa
stops.campa: Six years the discoverer of the South Sea and his rival governor Pedrarias Dávila circle each other with feigned marriages and real suspicion, until Pedrarias, believing new treason, sends orders to the fort of Acla. It is Pizarro, Balboa's own old comrade of the Darién marches, the man who knelt beside him on the ridge, who rides out and takes him under arrest without a blow struck, and delivers him to the judge who will condemn him. Loyalty to the governor who pays him outweighs the memory of the sea they discovered together; the ledger of this life keeps that kind of arithmetic from the start.

stops.name: Panamá, the founding of the city, alcalde
stops.campa: On the Pacific shore Pedrarias founds the city of Panamá, hinge between the two seas and the last Spanish town before whatever lies south along the coast Balboa opened. Pizarro is granted land on the Chagres and, for his service against Balboa, the office of alcalde: mayor and magistrate of the new city, 1519 to 1523. It is respectability of a kind he has never had: a house, an encomienda, a chair on the cabildo. He is past forty and comfortable. The rumors of gold to the south, which he has heard for a decade, have not yet made him move.

stops.name: Panamá, the Empresa of the Levant, the pact of three
stops.campa: In the church of the Mercedarians at Panamá, Pizarro signs the pact, the Empresa del Levante, with the soldier Diego de Almagro and the priest Hernando de Luque, who supplies what money there is. Each swears the enterprise to the south will be shared alike, gold, land, and rank, whoever bears the worse hardship. Pizarro is close to fifty, comfortable, an alcalde with land on the Chagres; he sets it all aside for a coast no European has sailed beyond the Gulf of San Miguel. Nothing in the rumor of gold has yet been seen by Christian eyes.
